---
title: Places and movement
jupyter: python3
---

Measles brought into one town doesn't stay there. People travel to the next town to work, to shop, or to visit family, and some of them carry it with them. Each town then has its own outbreak, with its own timing, and the towns' outbreaks are linked by the people who move between them. This is a metapopulation model: several populations, each mixing mostly within itself, coupled by movement.

This tutorial takes the measles model from one town to four. By the end, you will be able to:

- give a model several places, with their populations and positions;
- say how much people move between them, with a gravity model;
- read the results for each place, and see how an outbreak spreads from one to the next;
- see how chance decides whether, and when, an outbreak reaches a small place.

## The model so far

This is the model from [Vaccination and scenarios](t5_vaccination.qmd): measles in a town of 100,000 people in three age groups, most of them already immune, with 10 people infectious on 1 January.

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True) # Plots and tables suited to a notebook

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta = ss.par(0.14, bounds=[0.05, 0.5]) # The rate of infection per contact with an infectious person, per day

infection   = S >> E @ beta*I       # Infection, at a rate of β times the contacts with infectious people
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10) # Latent for 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)  # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
    init = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The share immune in each age group
    init_n = dict(I=10),                          # 10 people infectious at the start
)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]]) # Contacts a day, between age groups
settings = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')

sim = ss.Sim(measles, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.plot('measles.I')
```

## Several towns

The town, Riverton, has three smaller neighbors. A **geography** gives the places: their names, their populations, and where they are (here, positions on a map in kilometers, from which Starsim works out the distance between each pair):

```{python}
towns = ss.geo.geography(
    names = ['Riverton', 'Hillside', 'Lakeview', 'Fairfield'],
    pop   = [100_000, 40_000, 20_000, 10_000],
    x     = [0, 20, 35, 60], # Kilometers east of Riverton
    y     = [0, 10, -15, 5], # Kilometers north of Riverton
)
towns.distances.round()
```

Places are a stratification, as age groups are: `stratify(patch=towns)` splits each state by town (a "patch" is a place in a metapopulation model), so that each town has its own susceptible, exposed, infectious, and recovered people, and the contact matrix applies within each town. The populations of the towns give the population of the model, so `total_pop` isn't needed.

The outbreak starts in Riverton only. `init_n` gives the number infectious at the start in each town, with `ss.by()`, a value for each level of a stratification. Since this changes how the disease starts, the disease is made again from the same transitions:

```{python}
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
    init = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])),
    init_n = dict(I=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0, 0])), # 10 people infectious in Riverton, none elsewhere
)
```

## Movement between towns

Without movement, each town would be a separate model, and measles would never leave Riverton. How much people move between places, and where they go, is often not known in detail. A **gravity model** is the usual first guess: the movement from one place to another grows with the population of the place people go to (a larger town draws more visitors) and falls with the square of the distance between them. The amount of movement is given separately, as the share of their time that people spend in other towns, `away`. The disease is split by age, as before, and then by town, with this movement between the towns:

```{python}
away = ss.par(0.01, bounds=[0.001, 0.1]) # People spend 1% of their time in other towns
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})
measles.stratify(patch=towns, mobility=ss.geo.gravity(away=away))

settings = dict(networks=contacts, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')
sim = ss.Sim(measles, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.I.by('patch').plot()
```

The people of each town keep their home town, but spend a share of their time in the others (the movement is commuting), where they can be infected by the people there, and infect them. 1% of the time is about a quarter of an hour a day, or a day out of every three months.

The outbreak peaks first in Riverton, at the end of April, and then in each other town in turn: in Hillside and Lakeview, the nearest, in late May and early June, and in Fairfield, the smallest and farthest, in mid-June. Since the towns have the same immunity, each outbreak infects the same share of its town, about 9%. `select()` picks one place's result, as it does an age group's:

```{python}
round(sim.results.measles.infection.select(patch='Fairfield').sum())
```

## How much movement matters

The share of time away is the least certain number in this model. To see how much it matters, run the model with several values of it. `ss.parallel()` with `pars=` runs a sim once for each value given (a parameter sweep), labeling each run with its value:

```{python}
msim = ss.parallel(sim, pars=dict(away=[0.001, 0.01, 0.05]))
msim.results.measles.I.select(patch='Fairfield').plot()
```

With 5 times as much movement, Fairfield's outbreak comes about three weeks earlier; with 10 times less, about five weeks later. The size of the outbreak doesn't change: in this model, measles always reaches Fairfield in the end.

That last part isn't realistic. In an ODE, a small fraction of an infectious person can travel to Fairfield on the first day and start an outbreak there; in reality, measles reaches Fairfield only if a whole infectious person does, and then only if the chains of infection they start don't die out by chance. To see this, run the model as a stochastic model (see [Repeated runs and uncertainty](t6_uncertainty.qmd)), with little movement, many times:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(away=0.001), solver='binomial', **settings)
msim = sim.run(n_runs=30)
msim.results.measles.I.select(patch='Fairfield').plot(lines=True)
```

```{python}
fairfield = msim.results.measles.infection.select(patch='Fairfield').summarize() # The infections in Fairfield in each run
print('Runs with an outbreak in Fairfield:', sum(fairfield > 100), 'of', len(fairfield))
```

In about one run in ten, measles never takes off in Fairfield: either no infectious person goes there while the other towns' outbreaks last, or the few infections they cause die out. In the others, the outbreak comes at very different times, from May to the end of the year, when some are still going. For a small place that is weakly linked to others, whether an outbreak arrives at all is a matter of chance, and a model that ignores this overstates how surely it spreads.

## As agents

The same model runs as agents, each with a home town, with `n_agents=`. Here there is one agent for each of the 170,000 people:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=170_000, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.I.by('patch').plot()
```

Each agent has a home town, and is exposed in the other towns for the share of their time spent there, as in the compartmental model. The outbreaks spread from town to town in the same order, with the variation from run to run of a stochastic model.

## Real places

Places can also be a country's regions, by name: `ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1)` gives Kenya's 47 counties, with their populations, positions, and which share a border. Movement can come from a gravity model, from the radiation model (`ss.geo.radiation()`, which needs no parameters), from a matrix of movement you supply, or from a register of moves on given dates (e.g. of livestock between farms), and it can be commuting, as here, or migration, in which people move home. See [Places and movement](../user_guide/populations_places.qmd) in the user guide.

## Exercises

1. Lakeview's children are less often vaccinated: only 65% of them are immune. Give the share immune by age and town (`ss.by()` with both, multiplied together: e.g. `ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98], patch=[1, 1, 0.8125, 1])`), and run the model. How does Lakeview's outbreak compare with the others', and does it change when measles reaches Fairfield?
2. A campaign that vaccinates 80% of children under 15 in Riverton only, on 1 March (`where=(measles.age < 15) & (measles.patch == 'Riverton')`): how many infections does it prevent in Riverton, and how many in the other towns?
3. Replace the gravity model with the radiation model (`ss.geo.radiation(away=away)`). Which towns' outbreaks come earlier or later, and why?
